values.title: One DSD Team
values.intro: Colleagues working together to make equity part of everyday decisions, programs, and services.
values.body0: The One DSD Team brings colleagues' knowledge of policy, programs, eligibility, and everyday operations into the division's equity work. Members work with the Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant to identify barriers, examine practices, and develop useful improvements.
values.body1: Choose a decision or practice that matters to staff or people receiving services. Describe what happens now, who experiences it differently, and what the team needs to understand. Use an example without private or identifying information.
values.body2: Members can explain a process, review a resource, question an assumption, try an improvement, or connect the work with colleagues who need to be involved. Agree on a manageable contribution rather than expecting every member to do every task.
values.body3: Use relevant learning and evidence to examine the question. Develop a small improvement with the responsible people, agree what would indicate progress, and return to what happened. Keep useful changes and revise what did not work. A meeting is part of the work, not its final result.
values.body4: The team develops advice and practical contributions. The person responsible for a policy, budget, service, or staffing decision retains that authority. Agree who will receive a recommendation and who can authorize a trial before promising a change.
values.body5: A monthly rhythm is planned from January 2027, once the program is ready, alternating practical team work with open conversations and shared learning. The consultant or members can bring a topic. Participation is voluntary, with room to listen, ask questions, and explore more deeply when helpful. Confirmed arrangements belong in the team's collaboration space.
values.body6: Amplify offers voluntary conversation, connection, and shared learning. Its co-leads can bring forward questions participants agree to share and return updates. The One DSD Team considers the work that needs further attention without directing Amplify's everyday conversations.
values.body7: When reviewing a resource, ask whose work it supports, which task it helps with, what is missing, and whether the example reflects practice. A policy analyst, a supervisor, and an eligibility worker may need different ways into the same subject.
values.body8: Record the question, the practice being examined, relevant evidence, the proposed improvement, and the person responsible for the next decision. Include the next agreed check-in and what changed. Keep personal disclosures and individual case details out of shared notes.
values.body9: Choose a small number of shared priorities. Make room to decline or renegotiate a contribution. Periodically ask whether the work is useful, whose perspective is missing, and what support members need. Preserve unfinished questions when membership or responsibilities change.

values.title: Tribal Nations of Minnesota
values.whoAndWhere: Eleven federally recognized Tribal Nations share geography with Minnesota. Each is a sovereign government with its own name, laws, leadership, and consultation process. Urban Native people also live throughout the state. This page explains when staff should seek government-to-government guidance; it does not provide Nation-specific guidance.
values.whyItMatters: When work may affect a Tribal Nation, Native children, Tribal data, services, or land, contact the designated Tribal relations office or liaison before planning consultation or engagement. A general community meeting is not government-to-government consultation.
values.withinGroupDiversity: Each Nation is distinct. Do not infer a person's Tribal citizenship, community ties, language, or residence.
preferredNames: The Nation's own name (for example Red Lake Nation, Lower Sioux Indian Community)
values.nameNote: Name the Nation. Do not use a demographic count as a substitute for a government.
whatToAsk: Could this work affect a Tribal Nation, Native children, Tribal data, services, or land? If so, contact the designated Tribal relations office or liaison before planning consultation or engagement.
accessChecks: This referral page does not provide Nation-specific access guidance. Ask the designated Tribal relations office or liaison which process and contacts apply.
whoToInvolve: Before planning consultation or engagement, contact the Office of Indian Policy or current designated Tribal relations office or liaison and follow the required process.
Work with the Nation's government through the process it designates.
whatNotToAssume: Do not infer Tribal citizenship or community ties.
Do not place a sovereign Nation in a general community partner list.
Do not use general cultural information as a substitute for consultation with the Nation.
values.spotlightBody: Tribal Nations are contemporary governments as well as communities with distinct histories and cultures. Minnesota Indian Affairs offers a starting point for learning about those government relationships. Respect includes recognizing each Nation’s authority to speak and make decisions for itself.
values.reflectionBody: Before shaping a proposal, whose governmental authority and designated consultation process must guide the next step?
values.source0Label: DHS Tribal and Urban Indian Relations
values.source0Note: Use the current DHS contact and guidance before planning consultation or engagement.

values.title: Intercultural learning in everyday work
values.intro: Explore how culture, experience, and access shape everyday work—and how your learning can inform a conversation, a decision, or a change.
values.choice: Begin with a question that matters to you. Follow the path from the foundations, choose a useful starting point, or return whenever you want another perspective.
values.previewTitle: Find a path from learning to practice
values.previewBody: Begin with curiosity, explore different experiences, adapt your approach, and put what you learn to use.
values.idiBody: If you have an Intercultural Development Inventory (IDI) profile and development plan, use the goals you explored in your debrief to choose useful learning here. You can also begin without an assessment. These activities support reflection and practice; they do not assess your orientation or replace your individual development plan.
values.connectionsIntro: A question may lead to reading, a practical tool, a conversation, or a change in your work. These spaces offer different kinds of support.

relatedLinks.label: People, Access and Culture leadership in DSD

values.foundationsPurpose: A useful place to begin when you want shared language for culture, equity, and access. Our experience shapes what feels normal; another person's experience can reveal something we have not noticed.
foundationsObjectives: Separate an observation from an interpretation in a workplace example.
Identify one familiar expectation that may not work equally well for everyone.
Frame a respectful question that leaves room for the person's own explanation.
values.foundationsExample: A colleague pauses before answering. You notice the pause; you do not yet know whether they are considering their words, need more context, or prefer another way to contribute. A question gives you better information than a label.
values.foundationsPractice: Choose a routine interaction. Write what you actually observed, what you initially thought it meant, and a question that could help you understand it. Consider other explanations before deciding what to do.
values.foundationsReflection: Which part was evidence, and which part came from my own expectations?
values.foundationsEvidence: An observation, more than one plausible explanation, and a question you can use.
values.foundationsNextStep: Explore whose perspective could add something to your understanding.
values.perspectivesPurpose: Explore this when a familiar approach seems fair, but people experience it differently. Shared needs and meaningful differences can both matter. Learning about a community offers context; listening helps you understand the individual.
perspectivesObjectives: Explain how the same process can place different burdens on people.
Identify a perspective missing from a decision and a useful way to invite it.
Revise an initial interpretation in light of another person's account.
values.perspectivesExample: A team offers everyone the same opportunity to speak at a fast-moving meeting. Some colleagues contribute more fully after reading a question or thinking it through. A shared invitation may need more than one way to participate.
values.perspectivesPractice: Take one meeting, notice, or service step. Consider who it works well for, who may face a barrier, and whose experience could help you check that understanding. Invite input without asking someone to speak for an entire community.
values.perspectivesReflection: What did I understand differently after considering another perspective?
values.perspectivesEvidence: A revised question or participation approach, with the reason for the change.
values.perspectivesNextStep: Try an approach that responds to what you have learned.
values.communicationPurpose: Useful when you want to turn awareness into a more responsive conversation. Adaptation begins with the situation, the person, and the communication task. It includes checking preferences, making access possible, and adjusting after feedback.
communicationObjectives: Ask about communication preferences without assuming them from identity.
Adapt a question, format, or conversation approach to a stated need.
Check whether the revised approach helped someone understand or contribute.
values.communicationExample: A service conversation becomes difficult to follow. Rather than speaking louder or repeating the same explanation, you check what would help: a clearer question, a written summary, accessible information, or qualified language support.
values.communicationPractice: Choose a conversation or explanation you can improve. Ask what would make it easier to follow, adapt one part, and check understanding through the task itself. For interpreter-supported conversations, use the language-access resources.
values.communicationReflection: What did the other person's response tell me about the change?
values.communicationEvidence: A revised explanation or conversation plan and a specific way to check its usefulness.
values.communicationNextStep: Look at the process around the conversation as well as your own approach.
values.decisionsPurpose: Begin here when a policy, service, workplace practice, or resource decision is open to change. Connect what people experience with the rules, steps, and choices that shape those experiences. Consider alternatives with the people affected.
decisionsObjectives: Identify a decision that could change an access or participation barrier.
Compare alternatives using evidence and the perspectives of affected people.
Describe a practical change, the responsibility needed, and what would indicate it helped.
values.decisionsExample: People repeatedly struggle with a renewal notice. A clearer explanation may help, but the team also examines the documentation burden, available formats, and steps required to respond. The improvement may involve both communication and process.
values.decisionsPractice: Use the Equity Analysis Toolkit companion to examine a current decision. Describe the barrier, compare options, identify who can shape the choice, and agree how its effects could be checked. Use the original policy and toolkit for applicable requirements.
values.decisionsReflection: Did the proposed change address the source of the barrier, and whose knowledge shaped it?
values.decisionsEvidence: A reasoned option or draft analysis that names the change, available evidence, and questions still open.
values.decisionsNextStep: After a change is tried, revisit what happened with the people affected.
values.reflectionPurpose: Return here after trying an idea, or when you want another perspective. A useful reflection connects what you intended, what actually happened, and what you will keep or change. Conversation with a willing colleague can deepen that learning.
reflectionObjectives: Distinguish a completed activity from an observed change in the work.
Describe feedback or an observation without overstating what it proves.
Choose a specific adjustment or a question for further learning.
values.reflectionExample: You offered a written way to contribute before a meeting. More ideas arrived, but that alone does not establish that people had more influence. You also examine which ideas shaped the decision and invite feedback about the experience.
values.reflectionPractice: Return to your practice note. Describe what you tried, what you observed, and what remains uncertain. Keep a useful change, adjust it, or seek another perspective. Bring a question to a peer conversation if that would help.
values.reflectionReflection: What would I repeat, what would I change, and what do I still need to understand?
values.reflectionEvidence: A brief account of application, feedback or observations, and a next adjustment.
values.reflectionNextStep: Revisit any part of this path as your work and questions change.

values.title: DSD programs and services
values.intro: Understand the services DSD supports, the people and partners involved, and where equity can improve everyday decisions.
values.servicesIntro: Find the program context, a useful question for your work, and a direct route to guidance.
values.peopleHeading: People and partners at the center.
values.practiceIntro: The Equity Outcome Map provides the shared foundation. The six ADSA implementation goals connect that purpose to practical work in the Aging and Disability Services Administration.
values.prioritiesIntro: The division overview identifies these risks and executive watch items. The questions below help directors, managers, supervisors, and staff connect each priority to people, access, and outcomes.
people: People with disabilities across the lifespan, along with their families, caregivers, and supporters.
Lead agencies, providers, direct support professionals, advocacy organizations, and other service partners.
engage: Program or policy concerns related to disability services.
Legislative issues affecting disability programs or service delivery.
Federal compliance matters requiring a DHS response or coordination.
High-impact issues involving people, communities, or partners that need executive awareness or a decision.
contacts: MnCHOICES, CFSS, and SEIU — Mary Lenertz
Waiver services and standards — Leigh Ann Ahmad
Rates Framework and WMS — Sharla Scullen
Disability Hub MN and E1MN — Lesli Kerkhoff
values.sourceNote: Division responsibilities, priorities, and named contacts are drawn from the division overview supplied October 12, 2026. Program links and the CFSS transition guidance were checked October 14, 2026. Use current DHS guidance for program requirements and confirm current staff assignments when routing a question.
directionItems: Set statewide policy direction for HCBS disability waiver and state plan services.
Oversee eligibility, assessment, support planning, authorization, and support for service delivery.
Shape legislative and policy changes that strengthen disability services and outcomes.
qualityItems: Use data, technical assistance, waiver and state plan compliance, and equity to support quality and program integrity, including prevention of fraud, waste, and abuse.
Build capacity for person-centered practices and positive supports.
Advance best practices that improve service quality and outcomes.
operationsItems: Manage rates, data, technology, contracts, and collective bargaining.
Connect people to resources, identify navigation barriers, and bring community insights into improvements.
Manage the SEIU collective bargaining agreement to support consistent statewide implementation.
values.waiversIntro: Developmental Disabilities (DD), Community Alternative Care (CAC), Community Access for Disability Inclusion (CADI), and Brain Injury (BI) waivers support community living through services matched to a person's needs and choices.
values.waiversQuestion: Where do assessment, documentation, authorization, or provider availability create barriers to a person's preferred community life?
values.cdcsIntro: A self-directed service option within disability waivers. People have greater choice and responsibility in arranging supports that fit their goals. CDCS is also available through the Alternative Care program.
values.cdcsQuestion: Are budget explanations, planning assistance, and accessible information helping people exercise real choice?
values.home_careTitle: Home care and Community First Services and Supports
values.home_careIntro: Community First Services and Supports (CFSS), home care nursing, and skilled nursing services help people receive needed support at home and in the community.
values.home_careQuestion: Can people understand their next step, access help in a useful format, and maintain services through a transition?

home_careLinks.label: CFSS worked example and toolkit practice
DHS home care and nursing services

values.eidbiTitle: Early Intensive Developmental and Behavioral Intervention (EIDBI)
values.eidbiIntro: Early intensive intervention for children and young people with autism and related conditions, with learning and support for families and caregivers.
values.eidbiQuestion: How do language, provider availability, family experience, and referral processes affect timely access?
values.mnchoicesIntro: Minnesota's assessment and support-planning approach helps identify needs and connect people with long-term services and supports. Counties, Tribal Nations, and managed care organizations use it in their work.
values.mnchoicesQuestion: Is the assessment accessible, person-centered, and consistent, and whose experience is missing from the evidence?

mnchoicesLinks.label: DHS assessment and case management resources

values.hubIntro: A statewide resource that helps people navigate services, understand options, solve problems, and plan ahead. Community insights can help DSD recognize where navigation is difficult.
values.hubQuestion: Are people reaching useful help, or being sent between offices without a clear next step?
values.guardianshipIntro: Protective services for eligible adults. Public guardianship includes court appointment of the DHS commissioner as guardian for an adult with a developmental disability.
values.guardianshipQuestion: How are the person's rights, preferences, accessible communication, and supported decision-making considered?
values.technical_assistanceIntro: The Resource Center, Response Center, Regional Resource Specialists, and Partner Technical Assistance Centers help lead agencies and partners work through program questions and strengthen practice.
values.technical_assistanceQuestion: Are questions resolved consistently, and are recurring barriers informing better guidance and training?

technical_assistanceLinks.label: Find the responsible person or office
DHS lead agency and technical assistance resources

values.cfssPriorityDetail: Complete the transition from legacy PCA services while maintaining service continuity. The current DHS manual identifies September 30, 2027 as the extended transition deadline; that extension does not apply to people on Alternative Care or extended PCA.
values.cfssPriorityQuestion: Are people receiving clear notices, practical assistance, and coordinated follow-up before a gap in service occurs?

cfssPriorityLinks.label: Work through the CFSS notice example

values.assessmentPriorityDetail: Complete reliability and validity testing while planning the transition to future assessment and support-planning technology.
values.assessmentPriorityQuestion: What evidence shows consistency, accessibility, and meaningful support for person-centered planning?
values.compliancePriorityDetail: CMS findings and corrective actions may affect operations and federal funding. Coordinate the authorized response and make implementation responsibilities clear.
values.compliancePriorityQuestion: Who owns each action, what evidence is needed, and where could a change affect access or continuity?
values.spendingPriorityDetail: Waiver spending growth places pressure on state and federal budgets and long-term program sustainability.
values.spendingPriorityQuestion: How do proposed responses affect service access, people with different support needs, and provider capacity?
values.reimaginePriorityDetail: The direction and timing of future waiver changes remain important policy and implementation considerations. Connect planning and communication to current official updates.
values.reimaginePriorityQuestion: What is decided, what remains open, and how will people and partners be included before choices are settled?
values.capacityPriorityDetail: DSD staff, providers, direct support professionals, and lead agencies are managing multiple major changes at once.
values.capacityPriorityQuestion: Are training, staffing, time, and partner support sufficient for the work being requested?
values.decisionsPriorityDetail: Federal requirements, statewide technology governance, and cross-agency mandates are reshaping decision pathways. DSD expertise needs a clear route into direction and decisions.
values.decisionsPriorityQuestion: Who is authorized to decide, who contributes expertise, and how will the reasons and next steps be communicated?
values.workforcePriorityDetail: Lead agency case managers and contracted partners need the capacity and support to maintain quality and continuity.
values.workforcePriorityQuestion: Where are workload, handoffs, or staffing shortages affecting people's experience?

values.title: Equity Analysis Toolkit
values.intro: Examine how a decision may affect people differently, consider alternatives, and prepare for a conversation about what should happen next.
values.companionNote: These five steps are a program companion, not the official toolkit sequence. Optional practice does not replace the toolkit, required review, or engagement with affected people.
values.roleIntro: Choose an area to connect the example with your responsibilities. You can explore any area.
values.consequenceTitle: What this choice brings into view
values.draftIntro: Keep your actual work separate from the practice example. These notes support discussion; they are not an approval or a completed equity review.
values.draftPrivacy: Use a general description of the work. Do not enter names, case details, or other confidential information. Keep any copy only in a location permitted for your work.
values.draftRetention: Your notes disappear when you leave or reload this page. Print or save your draft before leaving if you want to keep a copy.
values.clearedMessage: Your draft notes have been cleared.
values.resourcesIntro: Open resources at any time. You do not need to finish a lesson or practice activity.
values.resourceIntro: The DHS equity policy and toolkit resource are available here without completing the steps. Follow DHS instructions for access to internal materials and any required review. This companion does not submit work to DHS or grant approval. DHS requirements should not be treated as requirements for every Minnesota agency.
values.scenarioNote: Use this example to compare choices and consider what you would ask before deciding. It does not describe an actual case or predict the results of a particular decision.
values.culturalContext: Community briefs can help you ask more informed questions. They do not tell you what an individual believes, needs, or prefers. Confirm preferences with the person and involve affected communities in real decisions.
values.authorityNote: The people responsible for the decision retain authority. A practice response cannot establish community agreement or replace direct engagement.
values.decisionIntro: Start with the decision itself: what is changing, what can still be changed, and who can decide. A clear scope helps people contribute while their input can still matter.
decisionObjectives: Write a one-sentence description of the decision.
Distinguish fixed conditions from choices still open.
Locate the related questions in the official toolkit.
values.decisionScenario: A service team is considering replacing mailed appointment reminders with text messages. Alex Rivera works changing shifts and shares one phone with Elena, who helps manage appointments and prefers written information in Spanish. What should the team ask Alex and Elena before changing the reminders?
values.decisionChoicea: Choose text messages now and discuss implementation later.
values.decisionConsequencea: In this practice continuation, Elena raises the shared-phone concern after the proposal has been presented as settled. Ask which choices remain open and whether people can still influence them.
values.decisionChoiceb: Define the reminder decision, its limits, and who can authorize a change.
values.decisionConsequenceb: The team separates the reminder method from rules it has no authority to change. It can now ask people about options that are genuinely open, while confirming applicable requirements with the person responsible.
values.decisionChoicec: Keep the existing process without further discussion.
values.decisionConsequencec: Another practice household reports unreliable mail delivery. Keeping the process also has effects worth examining; the team still needs to understand the problem and its authority to respond.
values.decisionDraftHelp: Describe the decision, what can change, and who has authority. Name any requirement that still needs to be confirmed.
values.peopleIntro: Look for differences in access, benefits, and burdens. Separate what the evidence shows from what you are assuming, and identify whose experience is missing.
peopleObjectives: Identify people who may experience the decision differently.
Name an information gap or missing perspective.
Write a respectful question to learn more.
values.peopleScenario: The practice records show that a text reached Alex's phone. They do not show whether Elena could read it in time. Another household member uses a screen reader, and a different household prefers mail for privacy. What information would you seek?
values.peopleChoicea: Treat successful delivery as evidence that the reminder was usable.
values.peopleConsequencea: The delivery record answers a narrow question. It cannot establish who read the message, whether it was understandable, or whether using it was private and accessible.
values.peopleChoiceb: Ask staff which reminder method most people prefer.
values.peopleConsequenceb: Staff describe recurring difficulties, which helps identify questions. Their experience does not establish each person's preferences or replace hearing directly from people using the service.
values.peopleChoicec: Combine available records with accessible conversations about preferences and barriers.
values.peopleConsequencec: Elena explains when she can access the shared phone. Other people describe different needs. The team has richer information but still checks who could not participate and avoids treating one family as representative of a community.
values.peopleDraftHelp: Note potential differences in experience, the evidence available, and whose perspective you still need. Avoid identifying individual clients.
values.optionsIntro: Compare workable alternatives, including the current approach. Consider who gains convenience, who takes on additional work, and what could make each approach more accessible.
optionsObjectives: Describe at least two feasible approaches.
Identify a potential benefit and burden of each.
Explain how an adjustment addresses a specific barrier.
State what remains uncertain before a choice is made.
values.optionsScenario: The team considers three approaches. In the practice example, Alex wants texts, Elena needs information she can read in Spanish, and another household relies on paper reminders. Choose an approach to examine, not a final answer.
values.optionsChoicea: Use text messages as the only reminder method.
values.optionsConsequencea: Alex sees a reminder quickly during a break, but Elena cannot access the shared phone when she needs it. The team must examine language, shared-device access, privacy, and alternatives for people who cannot use texts.
values.optionsConsequenceb: A household that prefers paper keeps its familiar method. Another household receives a reminder late. Keeping mail does not resolve all access concerns, and the team needs evidence about those remaining barriers.
values.optionsChoicec: Offer a choice of reminder methods and confirm communication preferences.
values.optionsConsequencec: Different households can request different methods. Staff then identify the work needed to record, honor, and update those preferences. Choice deserves examination alongside staffing, accessibility, privacy, and applicable requirements; it is not automatically the best answer in every setting.
values.optionsDraftHelp: Compare two or more approaches. Include possible benefits, burdens, adjustments, and uncertainties rather than predicting results.
values.participationIntro: Identify who should help shape the decision and what would make participation possible. Explain what people can influence and how they will hear what happened to their input.
participationObjectives: Identify who should help shape the decision.
Propose an accessible way to seek participation.
Assign a responsible person to a proposed action.
Explain how participants will hear what happened to their input.
values.participationScenario: Before recommending a reminder approach, the team wants to hear from service users. Alex cannot attend a daytime meeting. Elena would prefer a conversation in Spanish. Which engagement plan would you examine?
values.participationConsequencea: In the practice responses, people comfortable with that channel are heard more readily. The team has not established what people excluded by language, disability access, connectivity, or confidence with forms would say.
values.participationChoiceb: Ask an advisory group to speak for every household.
values.participationConsequenceb: The group contributes useful experience and questions. Its members cannot represent every household's circumstances. The team still needs to identify missing perspectives and accessible ways to hear them.
values.participationChoicec: Offer several accessible ways to participate and explain what remains open.
values.participationConsequencec: People have more ways to contribute, and the team plans language and disability access with participants. It still needs time, responsible staff, and a clear account of how input affected the decision. This practice cannot supply actual community agreement.
values.participationDraftHelp: Identify people to involve, participation supports, decisions they can influence, responsible staff, and how you will report back.
values.reviewIntro: Plan how people will examine what happens after a decision. Choose information that can reveal problems, name its limits, and agree on when the decision needs another look.
reviewObjectives: Identify an observable signal worth reviewing.
Explain what that signal cannot establish.
Name who will review the information.
Specify a condition that would prompt reconsideration.
values.reviewScenario: Suppose the responsible decision-makers authorize a limited change after the required review and engagement. The team now needs a follow-up plan. What would you recommend examining?
values.reviewChoicea: Count delivered messages and call the change successful if delivery improves.
values.reviewConsequencea: The count helps assess delivery but does not establish comprehension, access, privacy, or fair outcomes. It could miss a problem even when more messages reach their destinations.
values.reviewChoiceb: Wait for complaints before scheduling a review.
values.reviewConsequenceb: Complaints may reveal an important problem, but some people may not know how or feel able to raise one. Without a planned review, silence could be mistaken for evidence that the approach works for everyone.
values.reviewChoicec: Review several signals with responsible staff and affected people at an agreed time.
values.reviewConsequencec: The team considers delivery, reported usability, staff workload, and people not reached. It names the limits of each source and agrees what would trigger reconsideration. Those observations inform the team's judgment rather than proving that one change caused an outcome.
values.reviewDraftHelp: Name useful signals, their limits, a review date, responsible people, and a condition that would prompt another discussion.

supportingResources.label: Equity Analysis Toolkit resource and access details

values.leadershipContext: Consider the decision authority, unresolved tradeoffs, and responsibility for follow-through. Ask what evidence and engagement are needed before a direction is approved.
values.policyContext: Compare the reminder options, distinguish policy requirements from local choices, and describe uncertainty in the recommendation.
values.serviceContext: Consider what a person must do to receive and use a reminder. Record barriers for the responsible decision-maker without assuming authority to change policy.
values.managementContext: Examine staff capacity, consistent practice, and how staff can raise concerns. Identify the support needed to honor communication preferences.
values.workforceContext: Consider the skills, learning time, and support staff need to provide accessible service. Examine whether expectations create unequal access to development opportunities.
values.fiscalContext: Examine implementation costs and work shifted to households or staff. Identify resource questions without inventing cost estimates or assuming the least expensive option is the fairest.
values.dataContext: Distinguish message delivery from usable communication. Examine missing information, the limits of comparisons, and whose experiences the available records cannot show.
values.engagementContext: Plan how affected people can influence the reminder decision. Consider language, disability access, timing, trust, and how participants will hear what changed.
values.communicationContext: Examine whether each reminder is understandable and usable in the needed language and format. Plan appropriate translation, accessibility review, and review with service users.
values.equityContext: Connect a specific access barrier with the wider decision process. Identify responsible partners and how engagement and follow-through will remain part of the work.

records.review: Complete authored surface read. Explanations connect evidence, individual preferences, decision authority and practical next steps without unsupported guarantees. Existing source dates, staff names and program conditions remain source-dependent, not currently recertified. Toolkit practice renders through staged experience; inactive draft fields are not counted as published changes.
